summary: Specifies a simple protocol for establishing symmetric data channels between WebRTC peers, using a two-way handshake and allowing user data to be sent before the handshake completes.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8832 is the small protocol that opens a data channel in a WebRTC call. One browser says which kind of channel it wants and how reliable it should be, and the other confirms. The channel is built from a pair of streams inside the SCTP connection that already carries the call.

questions: how are webrtc data channels established
what is the data channel establishment protocol
how do webrtc data channels get opened
why do dtls clients use even stream ids
what channel types does dcep define
subtitle: How two browsers open a named, tunable message channel inside one SCTP connection, with a two-message handshake.

tldr.problem: A WebRTC data channel has to be opened before any application data can flow, and the two peers have to agree on its properties first.
tldr.mechanism: The Data Channel Establishment Protocol opens a channel with two messages: the opener sends a DATA_CHANNEL_OPEN carrying the channel type, priority, reliability setting, label and protocol, and the peer answers with a DATA_CHANNEL_ACK. Each side uses streams of a fixed parity, even for the DTLS client and odd for the DTLS server, so both can open channels at the same time without colliding.
tldr.outcome: A data channel can be opened with a consistent set of properties, and the opener may send user data before the acknowledgement arrives, which saves a round trip.

facts.label: Stream parity rule
facts.value: Even for the DTLS client, odd for the DTLS server

today: RFC 8832 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It renames the SCTP payload protocol identifier 50 from WebRTC Control to WebRTC DCEP, and it establishes the Data Channel Establishment Protocol Parameters registry with its message type and channel type tables. It is part of the WebRTC suite whose roadmap is in RFC 8825.

sections.title: What the Protocol Does
sections.content: The Data Channel Establishment Protocol is designed to provide, in the WebRTC data channel context, a simple in-band method for opening symmetric data channels. The protocol uses the Stream Control Transmission Protocol encapsulated in Datagram Transport Layer Security, so that DCEP benefits from the already standardized transport and security features of SCTP and DTLS. DTLS 1.0 is defined in RFC 4347, the present latest version DTLS 1.2 is defined in RFC 6347, and an upcoming version DTLS 1.3 is defined in the work on TLS and DTLS 1.3.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new travels on the network for this. A WebRTC call already carries an SCTP connection inside DTLS, and the establishment messages are simply extra pieces of data on that connection, with a marker that tells the two sides they are control messages rather than application data.

sections.title: Association, Stream and Data Channel
sections.content: The document uses three terms. An association is an SCTP association. A stream is a unidirectional stream of an SCTP association, uniquely identified by an SCTP stream identifier in the range 0 to 65534; the identifier 65535 is reserved because the SCTP INIT and INIT-ACK chunks only allow a maximum of 65535 streams to be negotiated. The stream identifier is the number that identifies a stream. A data channel is two streams with the same stream identifier, one in each direction, managed together.
sections.plainLanguage: A data channel is not a new connection. It is two one-way streams inside the existing SCTP connection, one in each direction, sharing the same number, and the protocol manages the pair as one thing.

sections.title: The Two-Way Handshake
sections.content:
The Data Channel Establishment Protocol is a simple, low-overhead way to establish bidirectional data channels over an SCTP association with a consistent set of properties. The set includes reliable or unreliable message transmission, where unreliable transmissions use the same level of unreliability; in-order or out-of-order message delivery; the priority of the data channel; an optional label for the data channel; an optional protocol for the data channel; and the streams themselves.

The protocol uses a two-way handshake to open a data channel. The handshake pairs one incoming and one outgoing stream, both having the same stream identifier, into a single bidirectional data channel. The peer that initiates opening a data channel selects a stream identifier for which the corresponding incoming and outgoing streams are unused, and sends a DATA_CHANNEL_OPEN message on the outgoing stream. The peer responds with a DATA_CHANNEL_ACK message on its corresponding outgoing stream, and then the data channel is open. DCEP messages are sent on the same stream as the user messages belonging to the data channel, and the demultiplexing is based on the SCTP Payload Protocol Identifier, since DCEP uses a specific one.

The opening side may send user messages before the DATA_CHANNEL_ACK is received.

To avoid collisions where both sides try to open a data channel with the same stream identifiers, each side must use streams with either even or odd stream identifiers when sending a DATA_CHANNEL_OPEN message. When using SCTP over DTLS, the method used to determine which side uses odd or even is based on the underlying DTLS connection role: the side acting as the DTLS client must use streams with even stream identifiers, and the side acting as the DTLS server must use streams with odd ones. There is no attempt to ensure uniqueness for the label, so if both sides open a data channel labeled 'x' at the same time, there will be two data channels labeled 'x', one on an even stream pair and one on an odd pair.

The purpose of the protocol field is to ease cross-application interoperation by identifying the user data being passed by means of an IANA-registered string from the WebSocket Subprotocol Name Registry. It may also be useful for homogeneous applications that create more than one type of data channel. There is no attempt to ensure uniqueness for the protocol field either.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening a channel takes two messages, and it works over the connection the call already has. The two sides avoid stepping on each other by a simple rule: one of them may only use even stream numbers and the other only odd ones, decided by which side is the DTLS client. Labels are not unique, so the same name can legitimately exist twice.

sections.title: The DATA_CHANNEL_OPEN Message
sections.content:
Every DCEP message starts with a one-byte field called the Message Type, whose values are managed by IANA. The DATA_CHANNEL_OPEN message is initially sent using the data channel on the stream used for user messages, and its fields are:

  • Message Type, 1 byte, holding the value 0x03 for this message.
  • Channel Type, 1 byte, specifying the type of data channel to be opened. The value 0x00, DATA_CHANNEL_RELIABLE, gives reliable in-order bidirectional communication; 0x80, DATA_CHANNEL_RELIABLE_UNORDERED, gives reliable unordered bidirectional communication; 0x01, DATA_CHANNEL_PARTIAL_RELIABLE_REXMIT, gives partially reliable in-order communication where user messages are not retransmitted more times than the Reliability Parameter specifies; 0x81, DATA_CHANNEL_PARTIAL_RELIABLE_REXMIT_UNORDERED, the same but unordered; 0x02, DATA_CHANNEL_PARTIAL_RELIABLE_TIMED, gives partially reliable in-order communication where messages might not be transmitted or retransmitted after a lifetime given in milliseconds in the Reliability Parameter, with the lifetime starting when the user message is handed to the protocol stack; and 0x82, DATA_CHANNEL_PARTIAL_RELIABLE_TIMED_UNORDERED, the same but unordered.
  • Priority, 2 bytes, the priority of the data channel as described in RFC 8831.
  • Reliability Parameter, 4 bytes. For reliable data channels it must be set to zero on the sending side and must be ignored on the receiving side. For a partially reliable channel with a limited number of retransmissions it gives that number, and for a partially reliable channel with a limited lifetime it gives the maximum lifetime in milliseconds.
  • Label Length and Protocol Length, 2 bytes each, giving the lengths of the two variable fields.
  • Label, variable length, the name of the data channel as a UTF-8 encoded string, which may be empty.
  • Protocol, variable length. If it is an empty string the protocol is unspecified; if it is not empty it names a protocol registered in the WebSocket Subprotocol Name Registry, and is UTF-8 encoded.
sections.plainLanguage: The open message names the channel's behaviour and its optional label. Six channel types are defined, from fully reliable and ordered, through reliable but unordered, to partially reliable with either a retransmission count or a lifetime in milliseconds. One four-byte field carries whichever of those two limits applies.

sections.title: The DATA_CHANNEL_ACK Message
sections.content:
The DATA_CHANNEL_ACK message is sent in response to a DATA_CHANNEL_OPEN message. It is sent on the stream used for user messages using the data channel, and its reception tells the opener that the data channel setup handshake is complete.

The message has a single field, the Message Type, of 1 byte, holding the value 0x02 for this message.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply is one byte long. Its only job is to say that the channel is open.

sections.title: How the Two Sides Behave
sections.content:
All DCEP messages must be sent using ordered delivery and reliable transmission, and they must be sent on the same outgoing stream as the user messages belonging to the corresponding data channel. Multiplexing and demultiplexing is done by using the SCTP Payload Protocol Identifier, so a DCEP message must be sent with the assigned PPID for the Data Channel Establishment Protocol, and other messages must not be sent using that PPID.

The peer that initiates opening a data channel selects a stream identifier for which the corresponding incoming and outgoing streams are unused. If the side is acting as the DTLS client it must choose an even stream identifier; if it is acting as the DTLS server, an odd one. The initiating peer fills in the parameters of the DATA_CHANNEL_OPEN message and sends it on the chosen stream.

If a DATA_CHANNEL_OPEN message is received on an unused stream, the stream identifier corresponds to the role of the peer, and all the parameters in the message are valid, then a corresponding DATA_CHANNEL_ACK message is sent on the stream with the same stream identifier as the one the open message arrived on. If the message does not satisfy those conditions, the receiver must close the corresponding data channel using the procedure in RFC 8831 and must not send an acknowledgement. This might occur if the message arrives on an already used stream, if there are problems with the parameters, if the odd and even rule is violated, or if the message is not well formed. Receiving an SCTP stream-reset request for a stream on which no acknowledgement was received therefore tells the sender that the setup failed. After also successfully resetting the corresponding outgoing stream, which concludes the closing initiated by the peer, a new open message can be sent on the stream.

After the open message has been sent, the sender may start sending messages containing user data without waiting for the corresponding acknowledgement. However, before the acknowledgement or any other message has been received on a data channel, all other messages containing user data and belonging to that channel must be sent ordered, no matter whether the channel is ordered or not. After the acknowledgement or any other message has been received, messages containing user data must be sent ordered on ordered channels and unordered on unordered ones. Receiving a message containing user data on an unused stream therefore indicates an error, and the corresponding data channel must be closed.
sections.plainLanguage: The control messages always travel reliably and in order, even when the channel itself does not. Until the reply arrives, the opening side has to send its user data in order, because the peer cannot yet know the channel is open. If anything about the open message is wrong, the peer closes the channel instead of answering.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The DATA_CHANNEL_OPEN message contains two variable-length fields, the protocol and the label. A receiver must be prepared to receive messages where these fields have the maximum length of 65535 bytes. Error cases such as using inconsistent lengths of fields, using unknown parameter values, or violating the odd and even rule must also be handled by closing the corresponding data channel. An endpoint must also be prepared for the peer to open the maximum number of data channels.

This protocol does not provide privacy, integrity or authentication. It needs to be used as part of a protocol suite that contains all of these things, and such a suite is specified in RFC 8261. For general considerations, see RFC 8826 and RFC 8827.
sections.plainLanguage: This protocol opens channels; it does not protect them. The protection comes from the DTLS layer around SCTP, and the receiver has to cope with a peer that sends enormous labels or opens as many channels as it likes.

sections.title: Registry Entries
sections.content:
IANA has updated the reference of an already existing SCTP Payload Protocol Identifier assignment and created a new standalone registry for DCEP with its own URL, containing two registration tables.

The PPID was previously registered as WebRTC Control. The name has been updated to WebRTC DCEP and the reference now points to this document, keeping the original date: the value is 50, with the date 2013-09-20.

The Data Channel Establishment Protocol Parameters registry holds the Message Types registry for the one-byte Message Type field and the Channel Types registry for the one-byte Channel Type field. New message types and channel types are assigned through an RFC Required action. The initial message type registrations are 0x00 and 0x01 reserved, 0x02 for DATA_CHANNEL_ACK, 0x03 for DATA_CHANNEL_OPEN, 0x04 to 0xfe unassigned, and 0xff reserved for future extensibility. The values 0x00 and 0x01 are reserved to avoid interoperability problems, since they were used in draft versions of the document.

The initial channel type registrations are 0x00, 0x80, 0x01, 0x81, 0x02 and 0x82 for the six channel types defined in this document, with 0x7f and 0xff reserved and the rest unassigned. If new channel types support both ordered and unordered delivery, the high-order bit must be used to indicate whether delivery is unordered.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol reuses an existing SCTP payload number, renaming it from WebRTC Control to WebRTC DCEP, and adds two small registries: one for the message types, which currently has just two values, and one for the channel types.
